title: Rates of Change & Trig Derivatives
summary: The derivative is a rate of change: velocity from position, and marginal quantities in economics. The trig derivatives $\frac{d}{dx}\sin x=\cos x$ and $\frac{d}{dx}\cos x=-\sin x$ (and the rest) extend differentiation to oscillating functions.

rate of change.plain: How fast one quantity changes per unit of another.
rate of change.in_class: The derivative; average over an interval, instantaneous at a point.

velocity.plain: The rate of change of position — signed speed.

acceleration.plain: The rate of change of velocity.

marginal.plain: The change from one more unit (cost, revenue, profit).
marginal.in_class: Approximated by the derivative of the total.

sine derivative.plain: How the sine curve's slope behaves.

speed.plain: The magnitude of velocity — always nonnegative.

concept_sections.heading: Derivative as velocity
concept_sections.explanation: If $s(t)$ is position, then $s'(t)$ is velocity and $s''(t)$ is acceleration. The sign of velocity tells direction; speed is its absolute value.
math_steps: Read direction from the sign, speed from $|v|$.

concept_sections.heading: Marginal quantities
concept_sections.explanation: In economics the derivative of a total (cost, revenue, profit) is the marginal quantity — roughly the effect of one more unit. Marginal cost is $C'(x)$.
math_steps: Model the total as a function of quantity.
Differentiate to get the marginal function.
Evaluate to estimate the next-unit effect.

concept_sections.heading: Derivatives of sine and cosine
concept_sections.explanation: The sine and cosine trade places under differentiation: $\frac{d}{dx}\sin x=\cos x$ and $\frac{d}{dx}\cos x=-\sin x$. The minus sign on cosine is essential.
math_steps: Differentiate term by term with the other rules.
Keep the negative sign on the cosine derivative.

concept_sections.heading: Other trig derivatives
concept_sections.explanation: From the quotient rule: $\frac{d}{dx}\tan x=\sec^2 x$, $\frac{d}{dx}\sec x=\sec x\tan x$, and the co-functions carry minus signs.
math_steps: Write $\tan=\sin/\cos$ and apply the quotient rule if you forget.

concept_sections.heading: Combining rules
concept_sections.explanation: Real problems mix trig with products and quotients. Differentiate $x\sin x$ with the product rule, and $\dfrac{\sin x}{x}$ with the quotient rule.
math_steps: Spot the outer structure (product or quotient).
Apply that rule, using the trig derivatives inside.

real_world_examples.title: A pendulum's motion
real_world_examples.scenario: A pendulum swings back and forth like $\sin(t)$.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Its velocity is the derivative $\cos(t)$ — fastest at the bottom, zero at the ends of the swing.

real_world_examples.title: Tides through the day
real_world_examples.scenario: Water height rises and falls sinusoidally.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: The rate the tide comes in is the derivative of a sinusoid — a cosine giving the flow speed.

real_world_examples.title: Marginal profit
real_world_examples.scenario: A company's profit depends on units sold.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: The derivative of profit tells whether selling one more unit still helps — marginal analysis.
